lessons.pregame_expectation: The number implied Indianapolis Colts +5.5.
lessons.actual_result: It graded a win. The reasoning behind it did not hold: 4 of 8 gradeable claims went the other way. The read of this matchup was wrong in its mechanism, not only in its number.
lessons.lesson: A winning number built on a reading the game contradicted. Nothing about this result should increase confidence in the mechanism EdgeDesk named, and treating it as confirmation is how a model gets worse while its record gets better.
lessons.suggested_investigation: Why did the number land while the mechanism failed? Either the number was right for a reason EdgeDesk has not identified, or it was luck. Both are worth knowing and they are different.

lessons.pregame_expectation: EdgeDesk published a fair total of 45.1.
lessons.actual_result: The game finished with 63 points, an error of 17.9.
lessons.lesson: A total missed by this much usually means a pace or a finishing assumption was wrong, not that both ratings were. Check which of the two moved.
lessons.suggested_investigation: Was the play count or the points per drive the miss? Both are in this game’s result record.

lessons.pregame_expectation: EdgeDesk makes it Kansas City Chiefs -0.7 where the market has Kansas City Chiefs -5.5 at FanDuel — a 4.8 points disagreement.
lessons.actual_result: Kansas City Chiefs won by 3. the side EdgeDesk preferred won, but did not clear the market number, so the market had the better estimate of the size
lessons.lesson: EdgeDesk was directionally with the market’s eventual answer but wrong about the size. The market’s number was closer.
lessons.suggested_investigation: Track disagreements of this size across the season. The question is not whether one landed; it is whether the class of them has any edge at all.
